title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
author: Abdulkadir Külçe, Alihan Esen, Cağla Fikir, Berke Kurt, Kuzey Arar, Gökhan Ercan, Faik Boray Tek
raw_text: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.
summary: This paper introduces echo, a locally-deployable agentic health assistant. an "agentic" system means it uses an iterative loop (like react) to reason, plan, and execute actions using various tools, much like a human would. echo also features temporal memory, allowing it to remember past interactions, and safety guardrails, which are vital for sensitive applications like healthcare. the local deployment aspect is important for privacy and control. for you, this paper showcases a practical application of llm agents, combining concepts like rag (through temporal memory), responsible ai (safety), and full-stack deployment considerations. you could try building a simple agent using tools like langgraph or langchain to understand how these components come together.
why: Showcases practical LLM agents with memory and safety, relevant for GenAI applications.

title: Google Captcha on Search, absurdities beyond belief
author: b112
raw_text: We all know how horrible Google search has become.  Yet beyond the issues with results, the need for quoting every search to find relevance, the nonsense shown without 'web' being used as an option?  It is now exceptionally slow.Searches, especially at 2am Eastern (a favourite time for night owls to work) take upwards of 10 to 15 seconds to return.  Yet these are also peppered with endless capchas, which sometimes require a checkbox but also 'what is a car', and 'is that a bike' nonsense.Yet we've seen over and over again, how LLMs can easily pass these tests.  I feel what I'm seeing here is more of Google's collapse.  Creating horrible search experiences for humans, without actually resolving any possible issues they're having with bots.  And it wouldn't be so bad, except these are repeatedly shown to the end user.  Each search.  With slow results, each search.What used to be beautiful, a sub second result, is now and endless break in workflow.  And you know what Google?  If I'm going to be handed this, why would I think "Gee, Google is exceptionally competent, I should use Gemini!".No.  I see a company barely able to manage its infra.  I see, frankly, pathetic response times.  I see an inability for a company which has the assets, and personnel, incapable of resolving immensely simple issues.  So why on Earth would I trust an LLM from a company that's devolving into "the screw up king".
summary: This news piece describes user frustration with google search, specifically its slowness and the frequent, often challenging, captcha requests. while not directly about ai models, it highlights a critical aspect of any software product: user experience (ux). even with advanced underlying technology, if the user interface is frustrating or slow, the product's value diminishes. as someone interested in full-stack development and deploying ai systems, understanding user pain points and the importance of a smooth, intuitive experience is paramount. it's a reminder that even necessary security measures need careful integration to avoid alienating users. always prioritize the user journey in your designs.
why: Highlights user experience issues, crucial for full-stack and deployed AI systems.

title: Scikit-fingerprints: Python library for scikit-learn compatible molecular fingerprints and chemoinformatics
author: Jakub Adamczyk, Adam Staniszewski
raw_text: We present scikit-fingerprints, a comprehensive, fully scikit-learn compatible library for molecular machine learning in Python, based on RDKit. Molecular fingerprints and related functionalities are workhorses of chemoinformatics, yet the widely used open-source frameworks are not compatible with the wider Python machine learning ecosystem based on scikit-learn conventions. scikit-fingerprints closes this gap, bringing molecular fingerprints, molecular filters, similarity and distance measures, applicability domain estimation, data splitting strategies, and more under a single, familiar interface. Scikit-learn compatibility means that an entire chemoinformatics workflow, from a raw SMILES string to a deployable model, can be assembled from composable building blocks and can reuse the mature tooling of the surrounding ecosystem. The underlying RDKit code makes it familiar and extensible for custom chemoinformatics use cases. We put a strong focus on unified interfaces, ease of use, computational efficiency, customization, and extensibility. scikit-fingerprints makes molecular machine learning faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy.
summary: scikit-fingerprints is a python library designed to make molecular machine learning more accessible by integrating chemoinformatics tools with the familiar scikit-learn ecosystem. it acts as a bridge, allowing you to use molecular fingerprints, which are numerical representations of chemical structures, within standard machine learning workflows. traditionally, specialized chemistry libraries like rdkits were not directly compatible with scikit-learn's conventions, creating a hurdle for ml practitioners. this library closes that gap, enabling you to apply your existing machine learning skills to chemical data, which is crucial in fields like drug discovery and materials science. understanding how to represent complex data, like molecules, for ml is a valuable skill. you could try exploring how different molecular fingerprints encode chemical information for a simple classification task.
why: Apply your ML skills to drug discovery and materials science.

author: alwa
